_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine -- Georgia rule seed, 2026-08-24. Loaded through add_rule.
Every provision below was read VERBATIM from Justia's published Official Code of
THE SERVICE-EXTENSION WORDING WAS READ FIRST, NOT DISCOVERED BY A FAILING TEST.
Texas and New York both turned out to use a period-lengthening service extension
rather than the federal after-expiry one, and the New York case was only caught
because a test failed. Georgia was checked before anything was seeded, and it is
the same shape: O.C.G.A. 9-11-6(e) says three days are added 'to the prescribed
period'. Three of the four states in this batch lengthen the period and only
Florida follows the FRCP order -- so the federal sequencing is NOT the American
default it looks like, and every future jurisdiction gets this read up front.
'OTHER THAN PROCESS' IS AN EXPRESS CARVE-OUT AND GEORGIA IS THE CLEANEST CASE.
9-11-6(e) extends periods running from service of 'a notice or other paper, other
than process'. Texas reaches the same result only by inference (Rule 21a(a)
excludes 'the citation to be served upon the filing of a cause of action') and New
York only by scope (CPLR 2103(b) governs papers served 'upon an attorney'). Georgia
says the words, so the 9-11-12 answer deadline carries no extension as a matter of
text rather than of reading.
THE E-MAIL LIMB IS IN THE STATUTE AND ITS SCOPE IS ACTIVELY CONTESTED. 9-11-6(e)
names 'mail or e-mail' on its face. Whether it reaches service generated by an
electronic filing service provider was litigated in Speckhals v. Golf & Tennis Pro
Shop, Inc.: the trial court held the three days did NOT apply to such e-service,
the Court of Appeals affirmed under its Rule 36, and the Supreme Court of Georgia
DENIED certiorari in 2024, with a statement from Justice Warren that the text 'does
not appear to support' that construction and that it would cause confusion across
Georgia. No binding decision resolves it. This engine extends for 'email' because
the statute says e-mail, and refuses to recognise a separate EFSP service method at
all, so a caller cannot get a silent answer to a live dispute in either direction.
A Georgia deadline computed from e-service through an EFSP should be checked by
hand until this is settled.
PROVENANCE OF THAT CASE, STATED PLAINLY: the docket, the cert denial, the Rule 36
affirmance and the substance of Justice Warren's statement come from published
case-law summaries and the Georgia Supreme Court's own denied-certiorari list. The
full opinion text was not read. Nothing computes off the case -- it is a warning
attached to a rule that is encoded from the statute's own words.
THE ROLLOVER IS TWO SENTENCES AND WHETHER THEY CASCADE IS UNSETTLED. O.C.G.A.
1-3-1(d)(3) sends a last day on Saturday or Sunday 'through the following Monday',
and separately sends a last day on a public and legal holiday 'through the next
business day'. Neither sentence covers a Saturday whose following Monday is a
holiday -- which is every Saturday before Memorial Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day,
Washington's Birthday and King's Birthday. The engine takes the CASCADING reading
(Tuesday), and the full reasoning, including the fact that this is the ONE place in
the engine where an unsettled reading was resolved toward the LATER date, is in the
standard's own comment in deadline-engine.js. Read it before relying on a Georgia
date that lands in a holiday weekend.
THE HOLIDAY LIST IS A FROZEN 2022 SNAPSHOT, NOT A LIVE FEDERAL REFERENCE.
O.C.G.A. 1-4-1(a)(1) adopts 'All days which have been designated AS OF JANUARY 1,
2022, as public and legal holidays by the federal government'. A federal holiday
created after that date does not reach Georgia through this subsection. See the
calendar file; do not regenerate it from a current federal list.
THE 45-DAY DEFENDANT PROVISIONS ARE THREE ROWS AND ONE OF THEM IS A DIFFERENT SHAPE
FROM THE OTHER TWO. This is the sharpest drafting difference in the Georgia set and
it sits between adjacent Code sections:
9-11-33(a)(2) and 9-11-34(b)(2) both say a defendant 'MAY serve answers or
objections within 45 days after service of the summons and complaint'. Permissive,
and measured from a different event -- so each is its own row and the defendant
gets whichever they choose to rely on. Same treatment as Florida's 45-day
alternatives, whose wording is nearly identical.
9-11-36(a)(2) says something structurally different: 'unless the court shortens
the time, a defendant SHALL NOT BE REQUIRED to serve answers or objections before
the expiration of 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon him.'
That is not an alternative the defendant elects. It is a floor that operates
automatically, so a defendant's real deadline is the LATER of the 30 days after
the request and the 45 days after service of process.
THAT SHAPE IS NOT EXPRESSIBLE AS A later_of MULTI-TRIGGER, and the first attempt
to encode it that way was WRONG and was caught by working the arithmetic by hand
rather than by a test. The engine's later_of resolves between supplied trigger
DATES and then applies ONE count to whichever wins. This provision needs 30 days
on one limb and 45 on the other, so the 'later of' ranges over two COMPUTED
PERIODS, not two dates. On a request served 2026-06-01 with process served
2026-06-20 the later_of row returned 2026-07-20 where the statute requires
2026-08-04 -- fifteen days EARLY, on a self-executing admission, which is the
direction that forfeits the matter outright.
UPDATED 2026-08-24: it is now encoded with resolve_periods, a real engine
capability built for this family, which computes each limb in full through the
same base-period code the main pipeline uses and compares the RESULTS. The
interim decomposition into a 30-day row plus a separate 45-day FLOOR row is
gone. That interim shape was honest but it left the combining step to a human
on the deadline most likely to forfeit a case outright, which is the wrong place
to require manual assembly. The engine now refuses unless both limb dates are
supplied. Georgia was the first user of the capability; Ohio App.R. 4(B)(1),
CPLR 5513(c), Tex. R. App. P. 26.1(d) and FRCP 15(a)(3) are the same family.
Reading 'may' and 'shall not be required' as the same thing would be wrong in both
directions, and the two sit within three Code sections of each other.
GEORGIA'S CROSS-APPEAL IS COMPUTABLE, WHICH NEW YORK'S AND TEXAS'S ARE NOT.
O.C.G.A. 5-6-38(a) gives the appellee 15 days from service of the notice of appeal,
flat. There is no 'or within the time limited by subsection (a), whichever is
longer' limb of the kind that makes CPLR 5513(c), Tex. R. App. P. 26.1(d), Ohio
App.R. 4(B)(1) and FRCP 15(a)(3) inexpressible here. So Georgia gets a real
cross-appeal row -- the first in this engine. Worth noting precisely because the
three jurisdictions before it all had to refuse.
NOT ENCODED, deliberately, and flagged rather than dropped:
1. O.C.G.A. 1-4-1(a)(2), days designated and proclaimed by the GOVERNOR. Unknowable
in advance, and Georgia's version is stronger than the equivalent limbs
elsewhere: the subsection REQUIRES the Governor to include at least one of
January 19, April 26 or June 3 or a suitable date in lieu, so at least one
uncomputable public and legal holiday is guaranteed every year. A Georgia date
from this engine is correct only absent an applicable proclamation.
2. O.C.G.A. 1-4-1(b)'s 13-day state-office closure schedule. A closure schedule is
not the statutory test; see the calendar file and the standing note in
deadline-engine.js.
3. O.C.G.A. 9-11-6(b)'s extension power, both the parties' written stipulation and
the court's order, including the excusable-neglect route after expiry. Note its
proviso, which is a real trap of its own: 'no extension of time shall be granted
for the filing of motions for new trial or for judgment notwithstanding the
verdict.' The engine cannot see a stipulation or an order either way.
4. O.C.G.A. 9-11-6(d)'s five-day motion-notice and one-day opposing-affidavit
periods. Both are real and both are lead-time minimums measured backward from a
hearing date, which is a shape this engine supports only forward; and the
one-day period would sit under the seven-day exclusion threshold, so encoding it
without reading how the two interact would be a guess. Named for a later phase.
5. The 'court may allow a shorter or longer time' clauses in 9-11-33(a)(2) and
9-11-34(b)(2), and the 'such shorter or longer time as the court may allow' and
'unless the court shortens the time' clauses in 9-11-36(a)(2). Court orders the
engine cannot see, and in 9-11-36 the shortening clause can displace the 45-day
floor that the multi-trigger row depends on.
6. O.C.G.A. 5-6-38(a)'s remaining content beyond the three periods encoded, and the
whole of the Appellate Practice Act's extension machinery.
7. Whether O.C.G.A. 9-11-6(e)'s three days reach a period fixed by the Appellate
Practice Act rather than by the Civil Practice Act. The annotations to 9-11-6
note that the Appellate Practice Act has no provision for computing time limits
and must be supplemented, which points toward the CPA rules applying -- but that
is an inference, not something read in either Act's text. NO extension is
attached to any of the three 5-6-38 rows, which produces the earlier date and is
the safe side of an unresolved question.

rules.label: Answer to a complaint after service of the summons and complaint (Georgia)

authority.quote: Except as provided in paragraph (2) of this subsection, a defendant shall serve an answer within 30 days after the service of the summons and complaint upon the defendant, unless otherwise provided by statute.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS, which is longer than Florida's twenty and New York's twenty and matches the federal 21 only loosely -- there is no reliable regional intuition here. NO SERVICE EXTENSION, and in Georgia that is the statute's own words rather than an inference: O.C.G.A. 9-11-6(e) extends only periods running from service of 'a notice or other paper, OTHER THAN PROCESS'. The summons and complaint are process. The rule's own opening, 'unless otherwise provided by statute', means another statute can displace this period entirely and the engine cannot see one. NOT encoded from this subsection: 9-11-12(a)(2)'s two 15-day periods, which are separate rows because each runs from a different event.

rules.label: Answer after the court denies a Code Section 9-11-12 motion or postpones it to trial (Georgia)

authority.quote: Unless the court sets a different time, serving a motion under this Code section alters the time for serving an answer pursuant to paragraph (1) of this subsection as follows: (A) If the court denies the motion or postpones its disposition until trial, the answer shall be served within 15 days after notice of the court's action;
authority.note: THE MOTION ALTERS THE ANSWER PERIOD RATHER THAN EXTENDING IT, and the new clock runs from NOTICE OF THE COURT'S ACTION, not from the order's entry and not from its service. That is a third distinct trigger vocabulary in one state and the engine takes the date as given without checking which of the three the caller meant. Structurally this is the same family as FRAP 4(a)(4)(A)'s retrigger, but it is encoded as its own row rather than as a retrigger clause because the caller must already know a motion was served and how the court ruled -- facts the engine has no field for. 'Unless the court sets a different time' is a court-order escape the engine cannot see.

rules.label: Answer after service of a more definite statement (Georgia)

authority.quote: If the court grants a motion for a more definite statement, the answer shall be served within 15 days after the more definite statement is served.
authority.note: SERVICE EXTENSION DOES APPLY HERE, unlike on the two rows either side of it, and the difference is exactly the 'other than process' line in 9-11-6(e). The 9-11-12(a)(1) answer runs from service of the summons and complaint, which is process. This one runs from service of a more definite statement, which is a paper. Same section, same act, opposite answer on the extension -- so the carve-out has to be applied per trigger rather than per rule family. Note also that this period runs from SERVICE of the statement, where its sibling in (a)(2)(A) runs from NOTICE of the court's action.

authority.quote: The party upon whom the interrogatories have been served shall serve a copy of the answers, and objections if any, within 30 days after the service of the interrogatories, except that a defendant may serve answers or objections within 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon that defendant. The court may allow a shorter or longer time.
authority.note: A REAL RESPONSE DEADLINE, unlike Ohio's and Indiana's designated-period floors and unlike New York's split between an objection deadline and a party-set production date. The 45-day defendant provision is PERMISSIVE -- 'a defendant MAY serve' -- and runs from a different event, so it is a separate row and the engine never chooses between them. Contrast 9-11-36(a)(2) three sections later, whose 45 days are a mandatory floor rather than an election and are therefore encoded as a later_of; the two wordings are close enough to conflate and mean different things. 'The court may allow a shorter or longer time' is an order the engine cannot see.

rules.label: Answers to interrogatories, defendant's 45-day alternative measured from service of process (Georgia)

authority.quote: except that a defendant may serve answers or objections within 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon that defendant
authority.note: A DIFFERENT CLOCK FROM A DIFFERENT EVENT, and an OPTION rather than a replacement -- 'a defendant may serve'. Where both are available the defendant relies on whichever they choose, and choosing requires knowing both dates and that the party is a defendant; the engine has no party-role field and does not decide. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: this clock starts on service of the summons and complaint, which 9-11-6(e) excludes in terms as process. Nearly identical in wording and treatment to Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.340(a)(9)'s 45-day alternative.

rules.label: Written response to a request for production or inspection (Georgia)

authority.quote: The party upon whom the request is served shall serve a written response within 30 days after the service of the request, except that a defendant may serve a response within 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon that defendant. The court may allow a shorter or longer time.
authority.note: A real response deadline, structured identically to the interrogatory rule including the permissive 45-day defendant alternative, which is again its own row. NOT encoded: 9-11-34(c)'s separate machinery for production from NONPARTIES, which runs on its own notice-and-subpoena timetable rather than on this period.

rules.label: Response to a request for production, defendant's 45-day alternative measured from service of process (Georgia)

authority.quote: except that a defendant may serve a response within 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon that defendant
authority.note: Separate row for the same reason as the interrogatory 45-day alternative: a different clock from a different event, permissive rather than automatic. No service extension -- the clock starts on service of process, which 9-11-6(e) excludes in terms.

rules.label: Answer or objection before a requested admission is admitted, party other than a newly served defendant (Georgia)

authority.quote: The matter is admitted unless, within 30 days after service of the request or within such shorter or longer time as the court may allow, the party to whom the request is directed serves upon the party requesting the admission a written answer or objection addressed to the matter, signed by the party or by his attorney;
authority.note: SELF-EXECUTING: the matter is admitted by operation of the statute with no motion and no order, the same shape as Ill. S. Ct. R. 216(c), Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.370(a)(6), Tex. R. Civ. P. 198.2(c) and N.Y. CPLR 3123(a), and expressly not the California shape. THIS ROW IS THE 30-DAY PERIOD ONLY. A DEFENDANT SERVED WITH THE REQUEST EARLY IN THE CASE GETS A STATUTORY FLOOR ON TOP OF IT and must use the separate later_of row (ga-ocga-9-11-36-a2-admission-defendant-later-of) instead -- relying on this row alone for such a defendant produces a date that can be far too early. The 'shorter or longer time as the court may allow' clause is an order the engine cannot see.

rules.label: Answer or objection to a request for admission by a defendant, the later of 30 days after the request and 45 days after service of process (Georgia)

limbs.label: 30 days after service of the request
45 days after service of the summons and complaint

authority.quote: but unless the court shortens the time, a defendant shall not be required to serve answers or objections before the expiration of 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon him.
authority.note: THE RULE THAT FORCED A NEW ENGINE CAPABILITY, AND THE ONE THAT ALMOST SHIPPED WRONG TWICE. A defendant's deadline here is the LATER of two separately computed periods: 30 days after service of the request, and 45 days after service of the summons and complaint. FIRST ENCODING was an ordinary later_of multi-trigger, which resolves between trigger DATES and then applies ONE count -- on a request served 2026-06-01 with process served 2026-06-20 it returned 2026-07-20 where the statute requires 2026-08-04, fifteen days EARLY on a self-executing admission. Caught by hand arithmetic, not by a test. SECOND ENCODING split it into a 30-day row and a separate 45-day FLOOR row and told the reader to take the later themselves -- honest, but it left the combining step to a human on the deadline most likely to forfeit a case outright. THIS ENCODING uses resolve_periods, which computes each limb in full through the same base-period code the main pipeline uses and compares the RESULTS. The engine REFUSES unless both dates are supplied, because resolving from one limb would be too early whenever the other governs. WHY THE LIMB WITH THE LATER TRIGGER DATE IS NOT ALWAYS THE ONE THAT WINS: the counts differ, so a request served well after process can still lose to the 45-day limb. That is precisely the intuition the first encoding got wrong. NOT AN ELECTION, A FLOOR -- and that is what separates this from the 45-day provisions in 9-11-33 and 9-11-34 three sections earlier, which both say a defendant "MAY serve" within 45 days. Those are permissive alternatives the defendant chooses between, and each stays its own free-standing row. Here the defendant "shall not be REQUIRED" to answer earlier, which operates automatically. A CAVEAT THE ENGINE CANNOT SEE: the floor opens "unless the court shortens the time", so an order shortening it removes the 45-day limb entirely and the 30-day row governs alone. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: one limb runs from service of process, which 9-11-6(e) excludes in terms as process, and attaching an extension that could only ever apply to one limb of a two-limb comparison is not something any rule text read here authorises.

rules.label: Notice of appeal after entry of the appealable decision or judgment (Georgia)

trigger_document.label: the date the clerk ENTERED the order or judgment on the docket
trigger_document.not_the: the date it was signed, decided, announced in court, or mailed to the parties -- those are different events and they bear different dates

authority.quote: A notice of appeal shall be filed within 30 days after entry of the appealable decision or judgment complained of;
authority.note: THE TRIGGER IS ENTRY. Five jurisdictions in this engine now start an appeal clock five different ways: Georgia from ENTRY, Texas from the SIGNING of the judgment, Florida from RENDITION, California from service of a notice of entry or 180 days from entry, New York from service of the judgment WITH written notice of its entry. Supplying the wrong one of those five produces a wrong answer the engine cannot detect. WHERE A MOTION FOR NEW TRIAL, A MOTION IN ARREST OF JUDGMENT OR A MOTION FOR JUDGMENT N.O.V. WAS FILED, this row does not apply at all -- the clock runs instead from disposition of the motion and is a separate row. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: whether O.C.G.A. 9-11-6(e) reaches an Appellate Practice Act period was not resolved from either Act's text, so none is attached, which is the earlier and safer side of an open question. See the file readme.

rules.label: Notice of appeal where a new trial, arrest of judgment or j.n.o.v. motion was filed, measured from its disposition (Georgia)

trigger_document.label: the date the clerk ENTERED the order or judgment on the docket
trigger_document.not_the: the date it was signed, decided, announced in court, or mailed to the parties -- those are different events and they bear different dates

authority.quote: but when a motion for new trial, a motion in arrest of judgment, or a motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict has been filed, the notice shall be filed within 30 days after the entry of the order granting, overruling, or otherwise finally disposing of the motion.
authority.note: A TRUE TRIGGER SUBSTITUTION, AND THE OPPOSITE OF TEXAS. Georgia discards the original trigger and restarts the clock from disposition of the motion -- the same mechanism as FRAP 4(a)(4)(A). Texas's Tex. R. App. P. 26.1(a) does NOT do this: it lengthens the period to 90 days while still measuring from the day the judgment was SIGNED. Two neighbouring states, two opposite treatments of the same fact pattern, and carrying either across produces a badly wrong date. Encoded as its own row rather than through the engine's retrigger clause because the caller must already know a qualifying motion was filed and when it was disposed of. Note the trigger is ENTRY OF THE ORDER, and that the disposition counts whether the motion was granted, overruled or 'otherwise finally' disposed of.

rules.label: Cross appeal by the appellee after service of the appellant's notice of appeal (Georgia)

authority.quote: In civil cases, the appellee may institute cross appeal by filing notice thereof within 15 days from service of the notice of appeal by the appellant;
authority.note: THE FIRST COMPUTABLE CROSS-APPEAL DEADLINE IN THIS ENGINE. Every equivalent seen so far had to be refused because one limb was a period the engine itself computed rather than an event date -- CPLR 5513(c) ('within ten days after such service or within the time limited by subdivision (a) or (b), whichever is longer'), Tex. R. App. P. 26.1(d), Ohio App.R. 4(B)(1) and FRCP 15(a)(3) all have that shape. Georgia's is a flat 15 days from a single event and needs no capability the engine lacks. NOT encoded from the same sentence: the appellee's option to file an INDEPENDENT appeal instead, which runs on the ordinary 30-day clock and is a different election, and the further requirement that the notice set out the title and docket number. NO SERVICE EXTENSION attached even though this period runs from SERVICE of a paper: whether 9-11-6(e) reaches an Appellate Practice Act period is unresolved (see the file readme), and omitting it gives the earlier date.
